{{Short description|Probability theory paradox}}

{{for|the similarly-named fluid mixing puzzle|Wine/water mixing problem}}
The '''wine/water paradox''' is an apparent [[paradox]] in probability theory.  It is stated by [[Michael A. B. Deakin|Michael Deakin]] as follows:

{{Quote
 | text= A mixture is known to contain a mix of wine and water in proportions such that the amount of wine divided by the amount of water is a ratio <math>x</math> lying in the interval <math>1/3 \le x \le 3</math> (i.e. 25-75% wine). We seek the probability, <math>P^\ast</math> say, that <math>x \le 2</math>. (i.e. less than or equal to 66%.)
}}

The core of the paradox is in finding consistent and justifiable simultaneous [[prior distribution]]s for <math>x</math> and <math>\frac{1}{x}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Deakin |first1=Michael A. B. |date=December 2005 |title=The Wine/Water Paradox: background, provenance and proposed resolutions |journal=Australian Mathematical Society Gazette |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=200–205 |ref=Deakin |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/252476141 }}</ref>

== Calculation ==
This calculation is the demonstration of the paradoxical conclusion when making use of the [[principle of indifference]].

To recapitulate, We do not know <math>x</math>, the wine to water ratio. 
When considering the numbers above, it is only known that it lies in an interval between the minimum of one quarter wine over three quarters water on one end (i.e. 25% wine), to the maximum of three quarters wine over one quarter water on the other (i.e. 75% wine). In term of ratios, <math display="inline">x_\mathrm{min}=\frac{1/4}{3/4} = \frac{1}{3}</math> resp. <math display="inline">x_\mathrm{max}=\frac{3/4}{1/4} = 3</math>.

Now, making use of the principle of indifference, we may assume that <math>x</math> is uniformly distributed. Then the chance of finding the ratio <math>x</math> ''below'' any given fixed threshold <math>x_t</math>, with <math>x_\mathrm{min}<x_t<x_\mathrm{max}</math>, should linearly depend on the value <math>x_t</math>. So the probability value is the number
:<math>\operatorname{Prob}\{x \le x_t\} = \frac{x_t-x_\mathrm{min}}{x_\mathrm{max}-x_\mathrm{min}} = \frac{1}{8} (3x_t - 1).</math>

As a function of the threshold value <math>x_t</math>, this is the linearly growing function that is <math>0</math> resp. <math>1</math> at the end points <math display="inline">x_\mathrm{min}</math> resp. the larger <math display="inline">x_\mathrm{max}</math>.

Consider the threshold <math>x_t = 2</math>, as in the example of the original formulation above. This is two parts wine vs. one part water, i.e. 66% wine. With this we conclude that 
:<math>\operatorname{Prob}\{x \le 2\} = \frac{1}{8}(3\cdot 2 - 1) = \frac{5}{8}</math>. 

Now consider <math>y = \frac{1}{x}</math>, the inverted ratio of water to wine but the equivalent wine/water mixture threshold. It lies between the inverted bounds. 
Again using the principle of indifference, we get 
:<math>\operatorname{Prob}\{y \ge y_t\} = \frac{x_\mathrm{max}(1 - x_\mathrm{min}\,y_t)}{x_\mathrm{max} - x_\mathrm{min}} = \frac{3}{8} (3 - y_t)</math>. 

This is the function which is <math>0</math> resp. <math>1</math> at the end points <math>\tfrac{1}{x_\mathrm{min}}</math> resp. the smaller <math display="inline">\tfrac{1}{x_\mathrm{max}}</math>.

Now taking the corresponding threshold <math display="inline">y_t = \frac{1}{x_t} = \frac{1}{2}</math> (also half as much water as wine). We conclude that
:<math>\operatorname{Prob}\left\{y \ge \tfrac{1}{2}\right\} = \frac{3}{8}\frac{3\cdot 2 - 1}{2} = \frac{15}{16} = \frac{3}{2}\frac{5}{8}</math>.

The second probability always exceeds the first by a factor of <math display="inline">\frac{x_\mathrm{max}}{x_t} \ge 1</math>. For our example the number is <math display="inline">\frac{3}{2}</math>.

=== Paradoxical conclusion ===
Since <math display="inline">y = \frac{1}{x}</math>, we get 
: <math>\frac{5}{8} = \operatorname{Prob}\{x \le 2\} = P^* = \operatorname{Prob}\left\{y \ge \frac{1}{2}\right\} = \frac{15}{16} > \frac{5}{8}</math>,

a contradiction.
